data.title: OCBC: AI rout becomes a growth shock as EM currencies take the dollar's strength
data.description:
If OCBC is right, dollar strength will be most visible in high-yielding and externally exposed EM currencies. That makes the case for selective EM FX hedges even while the dollar softens against the majors. Carry trades funded in low-yielders are vulnerable to further unwinding if the AI sell-off resumes, which could add volatility to Asian currencies, especially those tied to chip exports. A clearer Fed pause signal, along the lines JPMorgan's Kelly expects, would be the main thing that could ease the pressure on EM. Any repeat of last week's forced selling in metals would support the "growth shock" reading.

-
The AI unwind has stopped being just a rates story, OCBC says, and emerging market currencies are paying for the dollar's resilience.

data.title: JPMorgan's Kelly: tech correction overdue, stocks to bounce, Fed to hike once then pause
data.description: Kelly's one-hike-then-pause view gives bulls a counter-narrative to the hawkish pricing that has weighed on stocks and gold. If December's statement or projections lean his way, front-end yields and the dollar could ease. Waller's push for 50bp, or a clear signal of a January follow-up, remains the main risk to that view. November CPI is now a key data point: a sizeable gasoline-driven drop would strengthen the case for a pause. Kelly's flow argument (401(k)s, buybacks, wealthy buyers) suggests dips may keep attracting support, even if the AI valuation debate isn't settled.

data.title: Ackman urges Fed to drop 2% inflation goal for 3%, warns 9 December hike risks recession
data.description:
Ackman's post adds to a growing chorus, now including the Treasury, arguing against further Fed hikes. That could feed hopes of a softer message on 9 December even if the hike itself goes ahead. Rate markets are unlikely to shift much on investor commentary alone. Any sign that Fed officials are open to slowing the pace, though, would weigh on the dollar and front-end yields and support equities and gold. His SpaceX example also points to strain in credit markets, so corporate bond spreads are worth watching as a gauge of how much tightening is already in the system.

---

data.title: US stock futures jump over 2% in relief bounce, gold rallies, but Kospi slides nearly 4%
data.description:
The bounce looks driven by positioning and policy headlines, not by any change in the AI valuation debate. Rallies could fade quickly if cash markets in New York don't confirm the futures move. Gold rising alongside stocks suggests margin-call selling has paused, which makes the metal a useful real-time gauge of whether deleveraging pressure is returning. Higher US yields and a firmer USD/JPY show some haven demand unwinding, with the yen on the soft side in holiday-thinned trade. The Shanghai and Hong Kong open is the next test, given Beijing's new margin rules and the brokerages' talk of a bottom.

---

data.title: Goldman sees European gas halving to €45 in 2027, but a cold winter could push it to €150
data.description:
A credible path to much cheaper gas would ease pressure on Europe's energy-intensive industries and utilities' input costs, and could weigh on gas futures further out the curve even while the winter contracts stay volatile. For oil, Goldman's surplus view gives bears a medium-term anchor. The near-term risks still point higher, though, while Gulf disruption continues, so dips may be shallow until flows clearly normalise. Lower energy import bills would remove one of the structural headwinds that has weighed on the euro. Rate differentials with a hiking Fed are likely to stay the dominant FX driver for now.

data.title: Chinese brokers see a bottom and a broader 2027 rally after Beijing's support push
data.description: The brokers' calls point to two phases. Near term, rotation favours high-dividend defensives such as banks, insurers, utilities-style infrastructure and consumer staples like baijiu. In any rebound, beta should lead, through ChiNext growth names, small caps and technology. The combination of official support measures and upbeat state-linked research may limit downside in large caps in the near term. Without a pickup in leveraged and foreign inflows, though, rallies may struggle to stick. Moves in margin balances after 30 November and northbound flows will be the gauges to watch.

The AI winners may not exist yet, J.P. Morgan warns, as mega-IPOs flood the market
data.description:
J.P. Morgan's numbers push back on one popular explanation for the AI sell-off, that a flood of new shares is draining liquidity. That puts the focus back on valuations and earnings doubts as the real drivers. Strong household, foreign and buyback demand also suggests a deep pool of buyers if sentiment stabilises, which supports the buy-the-dip case. The point that much of the value creation now happens before listing is a caution for anyone chasing new AI listings, and it could weigh on post-IPO performance.

data.title: SNB's Martin eyes second-round effects after inflation jumps to 1.5%, hike in view
data.description:
Martin's focus on second-round effects is a hawkish signal, and it supports pricing for a December SNB hike. A tightening Swiss central bank alongside a hiking Fed changes the usual rate-differential story for the franc. Combined with strong safe-haven demand during the equity rout, that could keep the franc well bid, especially against the euro. That is the very currency risk Martin flagged, so the SNB may stay willing to lean against excessive franc strength even as it tightens. UBS shares remain exposed to headlines on the capital rules and any further talk of a headquarters move.

---

data.title: Gold sinks 9% in a week as margin calls and Fed hike bets override its haven role
data.description:
Gold is currently trading as a funding asset, so its near-term direction depends more on equity volatility and leveraged positioning than on traditional safe-haven demand. A December Fed hike is close to fully priced, so further downside from rates alone may be limited. The bigger risk is another wave of liquidation if the AI sell-off deepens. Spot is now far below every major bank's year-end target, so forecast cuts could keep coming, which may weigh on sentiment even if outright selling slows. A sustained halt in equity losses is likely to be the first trigger for bargain hunting.

---

data.title: Korea's market rescue fund is worth around $8 billion, but is 10.76 trillion won enough?
data.description:
The fund's size makes it more of a confidence signal than a market mover, so traders are likely to watch how quickly and how visibly it is deployed, not just its headline value. If it is activated and the selling doesn't slow, pressure could build for a larger fund or for the outright short-selling curbs that authorities have so far avoided. Heavy foreign short positioning also leaves room for sharp short-covering rallies if sentiment turns, which could make Kospi swings even wider in both directions this week. Any further weakness in Korean equities may also feed through to the won via foreign outflows.

---

data.title: Could Nvidia shareholders force Huang back? The 15% hurdle behind a long-shot idea
data.description:
For now this is a watch item, not a trading catalyst. There's no filing, no coalition and a board that has firmly closed the door. If it did escalate into a formal fight, the leadership uncertainty would likely weigh on Nvidia shares in the near term, whatever the outcome, at a time when AI stocks are already under heavy pressure. Some investors would treat a credible path back for Huang as positive for strategic continuity, which is why any SEC filings showing coordinated holders would draw immediate attention. The export compliance review is still the more important driver for the stock.

---

data.title: Bessent leaves door open to Huang return at Nvidia, a week after urging an outside CEO
data.description: Removing Washington's apparent veto on Huang lowers one source of leadership uncertainty at the world's most important AI chipmaker, which could ease some of the pressure on Nvidia after last week's slide. The bigger regulatory overhang is still there, though. Any finding of export-control breaches could bring penalties or tighter limits on China-linked sales, which would hit revenue expectations directly. Traders are likely to treat the board's compliance response as a binary event for the stock and for AI sentiment more broadly. A clean answer would also strengthen the case for a Huang return.

data.title: China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work?
data.description:
The margin cut may help mainland sentiment at the open, especially in the high-beta growth names on ChiNext and the STAR board, where leveraged retail money tends to concentrate. Because the change only takes effect on 30 November, its direct flow impact is a week away, so traders may treat early gains as anticipatory and easy to reverse. Hong Kong-listed Chinese tech is outside the scope of the measures and stays more exposed to the global AI rout. The yuan is unlikely to react much unless the measures bring clear inflows back into mainland equities.

----

data.title: Australia flash PMI sinks to 46.1 as private sector shrinks at fastest pace in 5 years
data.description:
A drop this deep, alongside the first easing in input cost inflation for months, weakens the case for further Australian monetary tightening. That leaves the Australian dollar exposed if rate markets start pricing a gentler path. The sharp fall in new export orders also points to softening external demand, at a time when global equities are already under heavy pressure. Prices are still running above their long-run averages, though, so policymakers are unlikely to move quickly to declare inflation beaten. Traders may also treat the flash reading cautiously until the final data in early December.

---
Higher interest rates are now hitting Australian demand across the board: services have joined manufacturing in contraction, new orders are at a five-year low and confidence is draining away.

data.title: Goldman names 3 signals that could mark a bottom as the S&P 500 sits 12% below its record
data.description:
Goldman's positioning data suggests that last week's rout cleared out mainly the fast money. Mutual funds, ETF buyers and asset managers are still heavily long, which leaves room for more forced or discretionary selling before any bottom forms. A December hike is close to fully priced and no Fed pivot is in sight, so AI earnings news is the most likely of the three catalysts to change the picture. The shift toward a growth downgrade favours defensive sectors and government bonds over cyclicals. It could also weigh on demand-sensitive commodities if it persists.

---

data.title: New Zealand retail volumes jump 2.2% in Q3, more than four times the expected pace
data.description:
A beat of this size is supportive for the New Zealand dollar and should firm rate expectations at the margin, since it weakens the case that NZ consumers need more help. Any boost may be short-lived, though, with global risk appetite under heavy pressure after last week's Wall Street rout. A high-beta currency like the kiwi tends to follow broader sentiment in that kind of market. Liquidity is also thinner than usual with Tokyo closed, which can exaggerate the first move in either direction.

----
